utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-R77.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, yesterday afternoon we had just moved on to the stage where you told us you were telling us about collecting witness statements in preparation of your defence for these proceedings. Did you take a witness statement from Jasna Marosevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was she, prior to making that witness statement, shown any of the witness statements shown by Witness Agnes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was she told the details of the allegations made against you and/or Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Drago Vukovic, did you take a witness statement from him?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but he wrote his own statement and after that it was typed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was he shown any of the witness statements made by Witness Agnes prior to making his witness statement or indeed at any other time?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was he told the details of the allegations made against you and/or Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you take the witness statement of Mr. Goran Neskovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was he either shown witness statements or told of the details of the allegations made by Agnes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And lastly, can you deal with the same issues in relation to the witness Spasoje Pisarevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Also nothing was said to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I think in addition to taking witness statements, you have collected a number of documents from various public authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In corresponding with those public authorities, did you disclose Witness Agnes's real name or any of the details of the allegations he made?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I behaved fully in compliance with the ruling of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, we have seen, on a number of occasions in the course of this case, a blue bag. Can you tell us how it -- how you came first to know about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about the existence of the bag in September this year or to be more precise, on the 16th or the 17th, because I was away in Bosanski Samac for two or three days, and I learnt about it from Ms. Jasna Marosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When and where did she first bring it to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She brought the bag to the office of my colleague Spasoje Pisarevic and the investigator in the Defence team for Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Who was present when she brought the bag to that office?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there, Ms. Marosevic, and my colleague Tatjana Cmeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what took place in that office at the handover of the bag?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the bag had been brought to the office in the presence of Jasna Marosevic and Ms. Cmeric, a list was made of the things it contained, and those things were examined, during which Ms. Marosevic took out each object, described it, and this was entered into the record or the document that we have in our files. At the end, Ms. Marosevic or, rather, that list was read out to her and she signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to deal firstly with the bag. I wonder if you could have a look at this. Is this the bag that was produced to you by Ms. Marosevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What happened to the items taken from the bag after they had been described by Ms. Marosevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those things were placed in the bag by Ms. Marosevic, as far as I can recollect, in the same order in which they were shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what did you do with the bag after it was handed to you by Ms. Marosevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, with the bag and the contents that had been registered in the report, I took the bag to my office, considering it to be evidence and intending to bring it to this court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you at any time add to the contents of that bag?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you at any time alter or interfere with any document in that bag?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you, in fact, bring the bag to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A day or two prior to the beginning of the hearing scheduled for the 29th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the list compiled and signed by Jasna Marosevic, or at last signed by Jasna Marosevic, did you bring that to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When did you first bring it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same time as the bag. When I arrived in The Hague, together with the other documents that I had in my possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you show the list and the bag to anybody when you got to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bag and the list I showed to my Defence counsel, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Since then, or since the commencement of this hearing, where has the bag been stored?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bag was brought to the Tribunal, and it was in the Tribunal, as far as I can remember, from that moment, but we took it to our room during the adjournment, but the contents were not in any way interfered with in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you say "our room", what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to our hotel room.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I do move that bag formally into evidence now, the chain of custody having been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: With respect, I'm not -- we take the position that the bag has not been -- the chain of custody has not been properly -- the foundation for that has not been properly laid, and we would oppose its being moved into evidence at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Where is the break in the chain, if you could just point that out to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: With respect, it is our view that Ms. Marosevic did not have continual custody of the bag at all times. She said it was in her closet, but we've established that there is ample opportunity for persons to have access and control to the bag. We would submit it's simply not appropriate at this point, on the chain of custody, to have it admitted as my friend now seeks to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does that not go to the weight and not to the admissibility of it? What you have said does go to the weight, clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does it go to the admissibility of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps not, in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then is it not admissible?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: On reflection, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will be marked D6.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just before we leave the topic of the preparation of your own case, when you corresponded with companies and public authorities, seeking evidence from them, without being able to refer to Mr. Agnes by his real name, how was it that you phrased your letters to them?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I phrased my letters, in the case of certain correspondence which was not relevant for the proceedings, using very general wording, saying that I needed a certificate. For instance, if Milan Simic's firm existed in a certain building, I needed proof of that. So when taking that kind of a document which is in the public domain, there was no need to give any reasons because I am a lawyer and it is in my legal capacity to make such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you place a time frame on the information you sought in most cases?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean addressing the authorities, the institutions from which I was seeking information? I'm not sure I understood you quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. Did you seek information from them on the basis that you wanted to know, between two certain dates, whether an event had or had not happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the case of certain documents which were relevant for a particular time period, my request mentioned that time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, lastly I just want to ask you these few questions. Have you ever driven in the middle of the night to the village of Martinci?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of the night, no, except that once I had my return trip in the evening on the 28th. But I was driving towards Belgrade, as far as I can recollect. That was the return journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you ever hung around outside Mr. Agnes' house in the middle of the night --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- or fired shots in the air outside his house?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why would I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you ever asked anybody to do that on your behalf?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Have you ever made phone calls to Mr. Agnes' house in the middle of the night of a threatening or a mysterious nature?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. There was never any such need. I didn't do that in the daytime. Why would I do such a thing at night?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever have the telephone number of that house?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had the number of the mobile telephone of his relative. That is what I was told, that it was his relative's. And I was given that telephone number from Mr. Vukovic, as I have said, because he had received that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever put pressure on Mr. Agnes to say one thing or the other about what happened in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There is absolutely no reason why I would do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever offer him the sum of 10.000 Deutschmarks and a flat and a job if he was prepared to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. There was absolutely no reason or justification, nor did anyone ask me to do such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, let me see if I understand you correctly, Mr. Avramovic. You've told this Court that when you took a statement from Jasna, you did not explain to her at all what Mr. Agnes had alleged against you or Mr. Simic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you asked her to give a statement, what did you ask her to do?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told her that it was necessary for her, if she was willing, to tell me everything she knew about the contacts she had had with Mr. Agnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So as far as you're concerned, she did not know anything about these allegations at any stage prior to coming to court today; is that correct? Or coming to court yesterday, sorry.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not, and it was -- it suited me that she shouldn't know, regardless of the ruling of the Trial Chamber. It was extremely important for me to be able to take such statements, not only this one but others as well, without saying what was involved so that I would learn everything about contacts with that individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, then why is it that Jasna brought the blue bag to your attention at Mr. Pisarevic's office? What possible use would that be to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my visit in September in 1999 and talking to Ms. Marosevic, an informal conversation, she mentioned it to me. Until then, she had never mentioned it because I hadn't asked her about it, nor did I know about its existence. I just asked her about the contacts she had had with Mr. Agnes, and she told me about them. And then in September when I came to Samac on one of my visits and when I was preparing to come to The Hague, she told me that she had this bag. Naturally, my reaction was to ask her to bring me that bag and to ask her whether she was ready to accept us making a list of the contents if that was his bag. She agreed. She brought the bag to the office. In my presence and my assistant, as I have said, we carried out the listing of the items.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What possible reason would there be for you to discuss Mr. Agnes with Jasna after May of this year?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already told you a moment ago. The first reason was to take the first statement for the needs of the Defence. The second reason was that in July, again during my visit to Samac, she told me that she didn't feel safe, that there were threats, that she was receiving anonymous phone calls, and a statement was made about that, which was then filed with this Trial Chamber. And finally, as you yourself mentioned, in September, again during my visit, in an entirely informal conversation which had nothing to do with the case, she told me about the existence of this bag, because she knew I had taken two statements from her, but not knowing what the relevance of it was, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So the offer of the fact that she had Mr. Agnes's blue bag in her cupboard, as you say, was purely coincidence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. I am a witness of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Just for the sake of interest, what authority did you have to go through Mr. Agnes's blue bag?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My authority emanated from the fact that I have been accused in this Tribunal of certain acts, and I was under the obligation to prepare my defence and produce all relevant evidence to my Defence counsel. I considered this to be a relevant piece of evidence and that is why I took it. That is something that Ms. Jasna Marosevic certainly could not have been aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So your evidence, as I understand it, is that Jasna brought this bag to the office of Mr. Pisarevic, where you happened to be, but you, of course, have no idea where it came from, just what she told you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. I learnt about it on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's not the question. The question is: You have no idea where it came from other than what Jasna told you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She brought it from her house, because I was present when she went off to her apartment to fetch the bag, and we went together to Pisarevic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sorry. I understood that you told us that she brought the bag to the office where you were, but now I understand that you accompanied her to her house and you removed it from the closet. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That is a misinterpretation of what I said. From the Lotos restaurant where I was sitting with her, after she had told me that she had had this bag, with my car and with my colleague we went to her house. She climbed up to her apartment. She came back to the car, and together we drove to the office. That is how it was. I didn't go with her into the apartment. I just waited for her. As the appropriate place for doing such a thing was an office, we went to the office, and she physically brought the bag to the office. But the distance is perhaps 200 or 300 metres, and it is on the way between the restaurant and the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My original question to you, sir, perhaps you didn't understand my question, is: Apart from Jasna telling you that she got it from her house, you have no idea how it got to her house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She told me that Mr. Agnes had left it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: During the months of May to September, did Jasna ever try to make contact with you about the whereabouts of Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite understand your question. Could you be kind enough to repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, sir, as I understand your evidence, you had sort of informal discussions with Jasna throughout those months, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When you went to Bosanski Samac, I take it you would visit in the Lotos Cafe and you would meet with Jasna?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't go to see her, as is known in the course of the preparations for the Defence. I had other tasks I had to carry out in the territory of Bosanski Samac. And when I was in Bosanski Samac on one or two occasions, I did drop in to see her or I met her in the town itself. It is a very small town, and one can hardly avoid coming across acquaintances. Sometimes we met by chance, sometimes we met in the cafe where she was working.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My questions aren't complicated, I hope, sir. All I really need to hear from you is whether or not you met with her from time to time.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: During any of the those times when you met with her, either formally or informally, by chance or by design, did she ever ask you as to the whereabouts of Mr. Agnes or whether you had heard from him?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. During the first statement, I told her to tell me everything she knew about Mr. Agnes, whereas I was not in a position to convey to her any information about Mr. Agnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My question was: Did she make an inquiry?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And this is despite the fact that he had stayed with her for a number of times, according to her evidence, and had left this blue bag with her; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, you asked me whether from May onwards -- we are talking about the period when Mr. Agnes, as is known, was not in Samac, he was not there -- whether I, in contact with Jasna Marosevic, had spoken to her about the whereabouts of Mr. Agnes and whether she had asked me about it. My answer is: From the 7th or, rather, the 9th of June onwards until today, in fact, I have not spoken to her about that matter, nor did I give her any information along those lines. That is my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Fine, Mr. Avramovic. I'll move on. Now, as I understand your evidence, you admit that you went to Mr. Agnes's uncle's house at Sremska Mitrovica on at least a couple of occasions, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I went to the house of the relations of Mr. Agnes on the 28th of September and later on in November when I went with Mr. Agnes to the Mimoza Motel.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that on those visits that you made to the house that sometimes you were accompanied by other people and sometimes you went alone?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the first meeting that I had on the 28th of September, I was accompanied by Mr. Neskovic; and the following time, when I went together with him to the Mimoza Motel, I went alone in my own car.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when you met him with Mr. Vukovic, where was that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was in Sremska Mitrovica, in a restaurant or cafe called Bingo, opposite the law courts, in the sports hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your evidence is you did not go to his house on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. On that occasion, we did not go to his house. I didn't even know at the time where he lived, so that it was only then that I learnt of the village, the address, and other facts related to his place of temporary residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, what kind of car do you drive? Would it happen to be an Opel Ascona?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What colour is that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A metallic grey colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And does it have Belgrade plates?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to deal next, if I may, with what we can refer to as the lengthy meeting with Mr. Agnes, the one you described where you went to his house and you took notes of that meeting. You know the one I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That would be your second meeting with Mr. Agnes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just so that we've got the time frame correct, this is towards the end of September, the 28th of December [sic] or early October, somewhere in that area?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It was September, the 29th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you admit that you took a lot of notes on that occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say that I took a lot of notes, but I did make some notes, yes, the chronology of events, of facts, which he related to me on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But you say you did not use a tape-recorder on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During our conversation, that conversation, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you have a tape-recorder?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have an old tape-recorder/cassette player in my office, and I don't think actually it belongs to me personally. It was in the office, so that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you ever use such a tape-recorder in the course of your business and taking statements from time to time?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't use the cassette player for taking statements, but I can use it and I used to use it to convey some of the notes on conversations which I gave to my assistant to put into the computer, to file it, or to store it in some other medium. And I did this too when I was a judge, for example. My verdicts, my rulings when I worked in the ministry, I would dictate them into a dictaphone and then hand them over to my secretary to type out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your evidence, though, is that you did not use the tape-recorder on this occasion, even though Mr. Agnes says that you did; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not use a tape-recorder to talk to him directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you read back to him your notes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not read him anything of what I had jotted down. And I said yesterday that the talk between him and myself on the occasion was rather confusing because we were all hurrying to get back to Belgrade, and also I was aware of the fact that he could not supply me with any essential data which I was basically interested in, and that was why I scheduled the meeting for the 28th at his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, I appreciate the fact that you wish to give as full an answer as possible, but my question was really quite specific. I just wanted to know whether or not you used the tape-recorder, as he said you did. The answer, I take it, from all of that is, "No."

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you try to get a statement from him? Did you get him to sign a statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He did not ask ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you discuss with him that you would like him to give evidence in The Hague about what he had told you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you bring your notebook with you to the court proceedings today?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have several notebooks in which I record my notes on my conversations, and I think I do indeed have a notebook but it is not my complete documentation related to the preparation of the Defence case and the conversation that I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Avramovic, it will probably be good to know that I wasn't referring to all of your notebooks about the preparation of the Defence case. Quite clearly, what I'm interested in is the notebook that you used to record the notes of your conversation on the 28th or 29th of September with Mr. Agnes. Do you have that notebook?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have that notebook with me because the data on the conversation with him I have not saved, and I did not wish to save them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you not save notes of potential witnesses that you are writing notes about? What's the purpose of notes if you don't keep them?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Defence is a process, an ongoing process, and when you work on a Defence case, you collect and gather information. The position of a Defence case is far different from the Prosecution. My method is a method of work with people, which implies the gathering of information and having talks and conversations with people. As you well know, the territory of Bosanski Samac is a highly-sensitive area with regard to the subject matter discussed here at the Tribunal, and that fact alone demands that I have a process of thought rather than taking statements automatically, as I can only assume that the Prosecutor does when he approaches victims or when victims come to them. So the process of my work and the methodology that I use has been conceived in such a way that I gather information and have conversations and talks, and what I consider to be essential I retain, what I do not I get rid of, because if I were to save everything, I would be buried with all the notebooks. Now why do I do this? I assess the information I'm given, I evaluate it, and in time, with the passage of time, in the course of my work I'm able to judge what I feel to be relevant and what I do not feel to be relevant. And that is my general principle and attitude, not only with relation to Mr. Agnes but it is the way I work, and in this case as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, apparently you're speaking too fast for the interpreter. Try to slow down.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I'll try.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So as I understand it, you don't have any notes of this very vital conversation with Mr. Agnes. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not only with him, not only for Mr. Agnes. There are other people, and the notes referring to those people I have not saved. Some of them I still have with me, but I am thinking about getting rid of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And just so that I have it clear, you were in the courtroom when Mr. Vukovic told us about a lengthy discussion with Mr. Agnes on a Saturday afternoon. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And when he transferred the file to you, did you have any notes of his conversation with Mr. Agnes available?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I did not save any notes, nor did I receive any pertaining to that conversation, other than the fact that he informed me of the contents of the conversation that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So it was clear from his evidence that Mr. Agnes was considered an important-enough person for the Defence to know about that he accompanied you to go and talk to him and introduce you to him; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say the reverse and understand Mr. Vukovic to have said the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, did you or did you not go with Mr. Vukovic at a time when you were introduced to Mr. Agnes by Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you've told us, in some great detail in chief, about Mr. Vukovic telling you about his impressions of Mr. Agnes as a potential witness; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, before that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So is it safe to say that he thought, at least, that it was important for you to know as much as you could about Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, at that particular moment, as I was talking over the case, at my own request he agreed that I have an additional talk with Mr. Agnes because of the need to ask him some things which he did not have the possibility of asking him at the time, nor was he interested in them, and that is the persecution. And I mentioned that yesterday, and that is why that meeting was scheduled, because we could contact that kind of man for that purpose, as I did from October on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And all of this was done without the assistance of any notes from Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday in the course of my testimony, and I'm going to repeat it here today, that Mr. Vukovic's knowledge about the events talked to him about by Mr. Agnes was so modest that it would not have even taken up half a piece of paper, so I see no reason why I should exchange any documentation on that subject matter with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Anyway, the long and short of it, you have no notes and you don't have Mr. Vukovic's notes; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Mr. Neskovic give you his notes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Neskovic, as far as I remember, several days prior to our joint visit to the village of Martinci, got from me a -- in that same notebook, a note of mine that I jotted down pertaining to a talk I had on the 22nd of September in Sremska Mitrovica. And he, as far as I recall, used that same notebook to introduce certain corrections in the sense of possible questions to be raised in the discussion with Mr. Agnes, and I told him that I planned to hold that talk. So that was also written down in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, could I just have something clarified from the witness? He did, in fact, take notes of his conversation with Mr. Agnes. He doesn't have any notes now, the reason being that he got rid of the notes; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's what I was hoping to find out. I'm not sure whether I did. I'm still working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you answer that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so. Quite so, Your Honour. It was precisely like that, and as I said at the beginning. And this isn't -- wasn't only the case with Mr. Agnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We understand that. Now, just so that I'm clear, you had them and you got rid of them. That's it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. In October or perhaps somewhat later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay. Didn't Mr. Agnes, during the course of that discussion you had with him, give you the names of other potential witnesses that he may be able to contact for you, according to your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a question of three witnesses, and I mentioned their names yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you not have taken down their names in those notes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I do not have an address or an identification or any more precise detail on individuals of that kind, then I would have no reason to retain them in the notebook. And you yourself say -- you talk about him as a witness, but for me he was just an informer. So this was of negligible importance to me. It was -- he was saying that he knew those individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you wrote the names down. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can say that on that page where I jotted down the gist of our conversation, that I made a note of the names. Possibly I made a note of it on the lists that I looked through, whether ticking the names off of the people that he remembered, that he knew; although, I said yesterday that those individuals, for the most part, he knew by their nicknames, and it was difficult for him to reconstruct lists and help me to tell me exactly which individuals were in the primary school building. So I just ticked off each name as I came to it, the names that he sort of seemed to remember, that he remembered -- that perhaps he could get in touch with. But apart from Mirsad Sahanic, he did not have any details about anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you already knew about Mr. Sahanic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt about Mr. Sahanic from him. I personally think -- I don't remember exactly, but I do believe that Mr. Vukovic knew about that too. I can't be certain. But at all events, I learnt this fact, and I knew about it on the 28th of September when I concluded my conversation with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to move on, Mr. Avramovic. We've established you didn't bring a notebook with you because you no longer have it. All right. How about telephone bills?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I didn't say that. I didn't say that. I did not say that the way you have just stated it. I apologise, but I didn't put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, that's what I was trying to establish, Mr. Avramovic. Please correct me. Let's do it one-word answers to simple questions. Do you have the notebook?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the notebook. I have several notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you have the relevant notebook containing the entries of your discussion with Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have a notebook of that kind. I do not have the pages of it, the pages pertaining the conversation I had with him, and I explained this a moment ago. All irrelevant data I rip out of my notebook and throw them away. So they are notebooks with metal bindings, and I use them for my fieldwork. That's what it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. Let me rephrase the question, because we seem to be equivocating about words. You have the notebook which once contained pages upon which you recorded your discussions. You have since ripped out those pages but still have the balance of the notebook; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. But not only about Mr. Agnes, and that is the essential point; not only about Mr. Agnes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: It's not a point, sir. My point is you ripped those pages out and, therefore, you cannot bring them to court with you today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Phone bills. Do you get phone bills for the work that you do on your defence cases?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, let me say that I get telephone bills to pay from the post office, which sends them in to me in Belgrade. Is that what you mean? In that sense, yes, I do receive phone bills, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And please help me here. Do your phone bills record your long-distance charges when you call from Belgrade to, say, people in Bosanski Samac or people in Sremska Mitrovica or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer that question but let me just try to think for one moment. I do apologise. I do understand you, but give me a moment to think about it. Two telephone lines in the office in which I work are on the old exchange and cannot give you recorded information of that kind. The third telephone line, which was installed several months ago, has an up-to-date telephone exchange which allows you to receive records and reports on the telephone conversations you have had. If you have that in mind, then I think that what I have just answered is precise and detailed information.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So do I understand correctly that prior to a few months ago, the telephone network did not give you printouts of your long distance phone calls; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. Allow me to repeat once again, if necessary. There are technical possibilities only for one telephone line, and that exists only as of recently.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. I got that. Did you bill for your work on the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you have billed for your trip with Mr. Neskovic, with Mr. Vukovic, for your meetings with Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding meetings held, in September, on the 22nd and the 28th of September, I think that from roughly that period of time onwards I have not billed for that period. In fact, I think that because those trips were not carried out within the deadline set by the Registry, I was unable to bill for them, but I will be doing so. In the case of these trips, as it is Sremska Mitrovica that we are talking about, apart from bills for fuel that I may have, I have no other bills that I could submit to the Tribunal for reimbursement. But I do not remember billing for this, though I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, the time period that we're talking about starts over a year ago; is that correct? September of 1998. Is it your evidence that you have not billed for your time either?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I haven't submitted bills for the entire period of my engagement. If you have in mind expenses, there are other things, other bills that I compile on the basis my monthly activities. I'm talking about bills for business trips. That I haven't done, but I do have the necessary documents and I will be doing it. I will be submitting them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That was not my question. Pardon me for not being clear. Let me be explicit. Did you bill for the time incurred in all of your dealings with Mr. Agnes? In other words, the hour and a half to two hours that you spent at his uncle's house on the 28th or the 29th of September, in the trip in the park with -- I think it was Mr. Vukovic? All of the times you were spending time with Mr. Agnes on this file, did you bill for that?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did submit a bill for my monthly activities, and I submitted an invoice as my professional engagement. If that's what you have in mind, I have done that. I express this in hours spent on interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Would you have itemised with which witness you would have spent the time? Is it a detailed bill such as "hour and a half, Mr. Agnes," and then a location and a date?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had a methodology of work prescribed by the Registry, and I marked my contacts with certain codes, as is customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to move on to another topic, Mr. Avramovic. I'm conscious of the time here. You told us yesterday, I believe, that Mr. Agnes told you that he could testify that Milan Simic was not at the primary school; isn't that correct, what you told us yesterday? It's a simple question.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A very simple question. He said that he had some information about events in the school and that he would be ready to talk about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you told us about what he told you, that his evidence would be that he did not see Mr. Milan Simic at the primary school. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In effect, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you said that that testimony was not significant, in your view.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I explained why yesterday, and I can repeat and give those reasons again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No. Are you telling this Chamber that you felt, as the Defence counsel, that someone being able to say that he didn't see Milan Simic harm anyone at the primary school, in light of the charges that are against him, would not be of interest to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but you have interpreted this in your own words, and let me put it in my words. If somebody says that he hadn't seen Milan Simic ever in the elementary school, and Milan Simic himself says that he was in the elementary school, then such a testimony would be quite insignificant. In the context of other facts which I referred to yesterday, I assume that you yourself would treat such a person merely as a source of information and nothing more, not as a witness. Nor did he sign any kind of statement about it, nor did I ask him to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, you were aware that Mr. Agnes had been detained with the very people against whom it is alleged that these crimes were committed in the indictment; isn't that true? You knew that and accepted that, did you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, if he said, since he was detained with these very people, that he never saw Milan Simic at the elementary school in relation to these people, wouldn't that be of interest to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not bearing in mind the overall picture about the events that I described yesterday; that is, my definite position as Defence counsel for Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Okay, you're the Defence counsel, sir. Now, moving on to Mirsad Sahanic, you say that the purpose for continuing contact with Mr. Agnes was because he said he could put you in touch with other witnesses; is that right? That's the only reason you gave us for continued contact?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it continued contact, continuous contact, but that was the reason, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Shall we say "repeated contact"?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday two telephone calls in that connection.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, you've already told us that you had by then decided that you would not call him as a witness; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And therefore his only purpose would be to locate these other witnesses for you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly yesterday that when you were at the meeting at his uncle's house and he told you the names of a number of these other witnesses and that he may be able to locate them for you, that you told him that you would leave it up to him to decide whether he wanted to do that or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Here we have a witness who is offering you up these names on a silver platter, and you're saying to him, "You don't have to. It's up to you, if you choose." Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. I mustn't exert any pressure even on a source.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's not pressure, sir. Wouldn't you jump at the chance of getting him to; "Hey, by all means, by all means"?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I insist on it? It is up to his free will to do it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope we understand one another. It is up to him to decide whether he wishes to get in touch with somebody. I explained that yesterday, and I would like to make that very clear, that he himself told me that such contacts were an extremely delicate matter and that he would try. He offered to do it. But he added that it would be difficult to achieve. And why should I then, knowing that, having been told that, insist on something that he said himself was a sensitive matter and which I know to be sensitive even if he hadn't told me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So do I take it, then, that not only did you not exert any pressure on him to give you a statement, but you also cautioned him that he needn't do what he offered to do unless he really wanted to do it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I deal with everybody. That is my approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, I think I asked you this moments ago. Mirsad Sahanic, you said you heard his name for the first time from Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, that was on the 28th of September when we had that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You're aware, are you not, sir, that Jasna had already contacted Mirsad Sahanic, are you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At that point in time, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Hadn't Jasna already given you his name and address and phone number?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You now know that she was the one that got the phone number in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: In fact, as it turned out, Mr. Agnes didn't know where Mirsad lived, did he?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me on the 28th, I remember that well, that he thinks that he lives in Tuzla or, rather, that his family is in Tuzla and that he is somewhere abroad. I don't remember whether he said Germany or some other country, but that he had been told something to that effect. That I knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You were in the courtroom when both Jasna and Mr. Agnes told the Court that he got the phone number from Jasna; he had no idea where he was?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I see my friend on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I've studied the transcripts with some care, and the assertion that Mr. Agnes told the Court that he got the phone number from Jasna is misleading. I can draw my friend's attention to the passages where Mr. Agnes deals with this particular question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not sure if it's necessary at this point, if my friend tells me the words are somewhat different. I've paraphrased my understanding of the evidence, but I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, did you at any time encourage Jasna to make contact with Mirsad?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Talking to Jasna in October, I learned that Agnes knew Mirsad and that if he had promised to get in touch with him, he could do so. More than that, Jasna and me, we did not talk about that. At that time, I did not get from Jasna any information about her having a telephone number, or being in touch with him, or anything else linked to Mirsad Sahanic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: When did you find out that Jasna and Mr. Agnes had Mirsad's phone number?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't learn that throughout the period while I was working on Mr. Milan Simic's Defence, except that talking to Mr. Agnes at his request at the end of the year, I learned that he had learned that Mirsad was coming to Tuzla. Where he got the telephone number from, whether he personally found out or someone else, I didn't ask him and I wasn't interested in learning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You were encouraging Mr. Agnes to contact Mirsad, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't encouraging him. He offered to do so if I thought it necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Did you think it necessary?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it would have been useful, I felt, to get in touch with anyone who had been detained in the primary school, and therefore including Mirsad Sahanic. If he were willing and if he were to be a credible witness, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You needed Mr. Agnes to contact Mirsad and lure him into Bosnia, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was my source.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you're telling us that you were not aware that Jasna was also trying to contact Mirsad and lure him, through whatever ways she had of luring Mirsad, back to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, until these contempt hearings started.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, do you know whether calls from the Republika Srpska to Germany are expensive?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't give you a reliable answer because the prices differ from those in Serbia, I'm quite sure. I don't know how much they cost.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Long-distance phone calls are generally quite expensive, are they not, sir, in the area where you live?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly they are expensive. We must agree on that. It depends, of course, how long they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Was it clear, from your discussions with Mr. Vukovic, that Jasna was doing everything she could to assist in the Defence of Mr. Milan Simic's case?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was never my impression, nor was that what Mr. Vukovic conveyed to me, nor did I get that impression from my few meetings with Ms. Marosevic, not the kind of impression you have just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Then why, sir, would you have contact with Agnes through Jasna Marosevic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contact was established through Jasna Marosevic for the benefit of my colleague Drago Vukovic. That is an established fact. Later on, all my contacts with Mr. Agnes were direct between the two of us in the scope which I described yesterday. I do not see why Jasna Marosevic would be somebody I would need from then on as a person for contact, if I understand you well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So you deny that she was a contact between you and Mr. Agnes on many occasions?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to be very precise when talking about these things. The contact I had with her in October was a logical follow-up of my needs to talk to a person who knew him personally, and she was such a person. Drago Vukovic told me that, to talk to her about certain things linked to the credibility of Mr. Agnes and to collect information about that. From then on, my contacts were direct, as I described them yesterday. And never did I engage Ms. Jasna Marosevic for that purpose, nor did I make any particular requests of her. To be quite frank, I saw her only a couple of times throughout that period. Do not forget that I had a great deal of work to do, and I didn't have time, among the many contacts I had to make, for this particular contact which I'm not going to say was not interesting, but it was not overly significant. I had other sources of information, and I still have other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, sir, we know of at least a number of occasions where Jasna was present during your dealings with Mr. Agnes, one of which was in the Cafe Lotos that she testified to a day or two ago, when she sat down and had a drink with you and you moved off with Mr. Agnes to another office. That was one occasion; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're talking about April. About April. Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you had a meeting with Jasna over the blue bag. You've told us about that today.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that was not the context of the contempt hearing. This is another case altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you've heard Mr. Agnes tell the Court about all the contacts that he had allegedly with you and/or Mr. Simic in Jasna's presence. You heard him tell the Court about those instances. You deny those?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I heard it. I'm not only denying it but I think the whole impression given is like fata morgana. I really don't know where such an image came from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What do you mean by that, sir? What do you mean by that expression. I think it was "fata morgana."

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. As the Prosecutor somehow prompted me to say that I had listened to the testimony of Mr. Agnes, and everything I heard that relates to our mutual contacts is so unreal and so full of various numbers, dates, meetings, that it appears to be a product of a fanciful imagination. And I apologise for using this expression. Maybe it's not the best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, maybe on this note we could take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we take a break, Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, are you going to tender the interview which Mr. Simic had with the Prosecution that was referred to in the evidence yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't believe so, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, what do we do, we just accept that that is stated there, do we?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it may well be there is some means of accommodation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't mean the whole but --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- I think it may be important the way it was said or the context in which it was said, because my recollection was your client, your current witness, said that Mr. Simic had stated to the Prosecution that he had been at the elementary school on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think, if I may say so, it might help us if we saw the context in which that was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. It may well be that that's not achievable in a practical form until tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. That's why we're raising it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, just to clarify, do you have one more witness after Mr. Avramovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, there is one more witness. Then I shall move documents into evidence that have already been filed, but we've put them in a more digestible and comprehensible form, and then we will have to consider whether the evidence of Mr. Spasoje Pisarevic is in an admissible form as an affidavit or, rather, statement. I know there is an amendment to that Rule, that I've just seen this morning, and that should conclude the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The amendment to the Rule, unfortunately, does not come into operation until next Monday, and the Prosecution has already taken the somewhat technical view that we are bound by the Rules of Procedure and Evidence as they presently stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it may well be, therefore, that we have to consider briefly whether the evidence of Mr. Spasoje Pisarevic is currently in the form of an affidavit, because I think the crucial difference between the two Rules is the addition of the phrase "some form of statement." I don't have the Rule currently before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The Rule is amended to take into account what we were informed was the absence of any affidavits or any procedure for taking affidavits in the former Yugoslavia. The answer may be, of course, if the Prosecution really wants to rely on such a technicality, to withhold and tender it after next Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps I may have some clarification. I'm not quite clear on Judge Hunt's comment on the technical view that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It was a document which was filed yesterday in other proceedings in this trial, in which we had suggested that we should hear an application for provisional release upon the basis that the Rule which has been amended -- we took that into account but gave our decision after the Rule had been, in fact, amended and come into operation. There is a very solemn and long and rather dreary document filed in which we are reminded solemnly that we are bound by the Rules as they currently stand. That's why I described it as a somewhat technical point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. Just so that I was clear. I was at a loss in terms of something that perhaps I or my colleagues said during the course of this aspect of the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, but your colleagues have signed the document. They'll explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. But now I understand that this is something -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Happily, you're not involved in those proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I was a bit taken at a loss in terms of what I had done to -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Not so much at a loss as we were when the point was taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will take the adjournment for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Prior to proceeding with the cross-examination, if I may, may I clarify the position that I would like to take as senior trial attorney on this aspect of the case with respect to my friend's submission as to the introduction of the document from Mr. Pisarevic, I believe it was, Spasoje Pisarevic. I have absolutely no concern or problem with that document being entered. As a matter of fact, I believed, when I asked for the motion yesterday by way after housekeeping motion, that all of the documents that had been filed. It was my understanding that that document, having already been filed, would be one of the documents that would be moved into evidence. So just so that I'm clear, I'm not taking a technical approach to the introduction of that document. We're quite content to have it moved in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I see you are in your role as Minister of Justice. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You are commended.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may now proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm going to shorten my cross-examination, I'm sure you will be happy to know, but there are a couple of areas I want to still touch upon. I will also try and speak closer to the microphone. I understand they're having difficulty hearing me. Now, sir, you've told us that Mr. Agnes offered you his assistance in finding witnesses for Milan Simic. Isn't that correct? It was his offer?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, why do you think he would do that? I mean, you know that he was detained by the Serbs in Bosanski Samac for a number of months, and you know that it's alleged that Mr. Milan Simic was one of the people who was there at the camp; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Why would Mr. Agnes possibly come forward to offer to testify for someone linked to his captors? As Milan Simic's lawyer, does that make sense to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His wish to tell the Defence team of Milan Simic everything that he knew about the primary school was not anything strange for me. I didn't at any time -- regardless of the reasons that you have just brought up, which can be put forward with a lot of argument that an individual of that kind should not talk to the Defence counsel for Milan Simic, and that is what I came to understand when Mr. Vukovic conveyed to me the conversation he had had, that he did so voluntarily and wished to state what he stated to him and subsequently to me, it did not appear to me to be especially unusual, that is to say, that somebody who had been in the primary school should tell the Defence team something, of course, unless he was a Prosecution witness. As far as I was able to see from the list of individuals, there were lots of people who were not Prosecution witnesses, that is to say, people who had been detained in the primary school building and who would come forward to testify about the events that had taken place in the primary school. This wasn't strange -- didn't appear strange to me, particularly in view of the fact that for a given length of time, he had lived in the Republika Srpska. And I felt that this was acceptable, it was acceptable for me to hear him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So you found nothing surprising about a victim coming forward offering to assist one of the people who were his captors; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me be quite frank in answering your question. There are many people who can be considered victims who will, nonetheless, be witnesses testifying here. At least I can only assume that there will be.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But in terms of Mr. Agnes, what was in it for him; a job, an apartment, money maybe?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. It was a friendly relationship coming from Ms. Marosevic, from a circle of friends, from the people she herself knew personally, and that's what Mr. Drago Vukovic told me. And later on this really did turn out to be so. Possibly the motives were related to Ms. Jasna Marosevic, but I didn't delve into the motives more deeply. But as I say, it wasn't a great surprise to me that somebody did offer to come forward and tell the Defence something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Before I move on to the next topic, I'm just reminded, sir, that yesterday you said something about you had checked with a number of people about Mr. Agnes, including Prosecution witnesses, and I remember I objected at that point in time about the source of your information. Who were those Prosecution witnesses that you referred to? Could we have their names?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, that was completely incorrect. It was a completely erroneous understanding on your part about what I was talking about yesterday, what I said here yesterday. No, they were not my contacts at all with the Prosecution witnesses. I said something quite different, and I want you to understand that in very precise terms and that it be recorded in the transcript, that searching for the need to inform myself on certain issues which were to have given me a full picture and allow me to decide upon the status of Mr. Agnes, I had a certain number of talks in the town of Samac very shortly afterwards. These were not Prosecution witnesses. Quite the contrary. They were citizens who live in Samac to this day and who know Mr. Agnes, and it is from those sources that I received additional information. And one of these pieces of information was the piece I brought up here yesterday, and that is that there was knowledge to the fact that Mr. Agnes, during his detention period, was in conflict with other detainees. And he himself told me that the local -- if I can use that word -- detainees from Samac were not very nice to people who had come in from elsewhere, from other territories or from other towns, and it was in that sense that it seems he had a conflict with them. And according to the information that I received, it boiled down to the fact that a number of these detainees or several individuals beat him up or quarrelled with him with respect to certain events that had taken place during the detention period. And so I followed along this logically and thought that if these individuals were possibly witnesses for the Prosecution, because I didn't know who these individuals were, then quite certainly Mr. Agnes, as a Defence witness, would not be credible because possibly people could have known this and then checked out the credibility of my witness, for example, if I were to put him forward. So it is in that context that I said what I did yesterday. So it is a piece of information that reached me. Of course, it need not be a correct piece of information. But on the basis of that information, I was able to make a decision as to the credibility of somebody who would one day make me a statement and that I could perhaps put forward as a potential witness for Mr. Milan Simic. So that is the essence of what I was trying to say yesterday here in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So is that a long way of telling me you don't have the names of witnesses for me?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The witnesses that I received information from, you mean? Well, I can, of course, give you them. There isn't a problem there. But I see no reason why I should here. Let me be quite frank. I'll tell the Trial Chamber -- I'm willing to tell the Trial Chamber everything. One of the people I talked to was my investigator, Mr. Spasoje Pisarevic, who had this kind of information given him, and he drew my attention to it. Of course, he did not check it out either, and that is why I said that it was a piece of information which need not be true, need not be correct. But it allowed me to make my own conclusions. And I had some other very strong arguments leading me to decide that I should treat this individual as an informer and not as a witness or potential witness. So that is what I know about that subject. I had quite a number of talks with people in Samac, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Your source of information wasn't independent witnesses at all; it was your investigator and it was rumour and innuendo?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's like this: I make my own decisions on the basis of the evidence that I have at my disposal. But when I paint a picture of something, then you can believe me that I can also paint a picture on the basis of rumours and innuendo. However, if rumour and innuendo were the sole source of information, then I probably wouldn't have brought in that kind of decision. But I heard what I heard from Ms. Jasna Marosevic, and I checked out my information in the field, and all this indicated that an individual of that kind could not be a credible witness in the Defence case for Mr. Milan Simic, and so I made a definite decision and severed all further contacts with him in treating him as a potential witness in the case before this Tribunal. So that is what I can tell you about that particular matter at this particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, I want to move on to another area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ryneveld, I should like you to ask the witness. The witness has told us that he decided at a certain point in time not to use Mr. Agnes anymore as a witness due to the absence of credibility that he thought he had and decided to use him as an informer, as a source of information. Could you ask the witness what prompted him to use Mr. Agnes as an informer?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard His Honour's question. I will repeat it. What prompted you to use Mr. Agnes as an informer, if not any longer as a witness?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you a brief answer, although I do believe that I spoke about that yesterday. I had several pieces of information given to me by Mr. Agnes which indicated that it was an individual -- I was dealing with an individual whom I could not believe, whose credibility I could not believe in. He told me himself that he had two names, one name which he used during his sojourn in the Republika Srpska and the other name which he used while he was in Serbia. He himself told me that he had changed his name in a way as he put before this Tribunal, although I think when he told me about this change of name, he said he changed his religion as well, that is to say, that he changed his religion in church. And he also told me that he was a refugee. Now, I can consider myself highly competent at least in that area, because in the course of my professional life and work, I drew up and drafted rules and regulations relating to that subject matter and I knew that that was a lie. When he told me this, I knew for a fact that he had lied to me or he was lying to me, because he could not have been able to do that officially, above board, he could not have done that; not because he was a Muslim but because no individual who was a refugee in Serbia, even if he was a Serb or any other nationality, could change his surname, because refugees are not entitled to avail themselves of the right to change their surname. This can only be done by citizens --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Avramovic, you're moving away from the question. We already have a full page of the transcript on the screen, at least, without me getting an answer to my question. What made you, once you decided not to use Mr. Agnes as a witness -- that we have understood, but you maintained contact with him after that -- what was it that prompted you to use him as a source of information, and which kind of information did you expect from him, and did you get that information from him? That is the gist of the question.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you, Your Honour. I would merely like, as the Prosecutor has just asked me, to tell you of some details which made me decide that I wouldn't use him.
