First, the fact that he had committed a criminal offence on the territory of the Republika Srpska; next the fact that he was in the army of the Republika Srpska and for unknown reasons had stepped down from it; also the fact that Ms. Marosevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have to interrupt you. That was not what I wanted. We already have all that information. The Tribunal has heard all that through the very testimony and cross-examination of Mr. Agnes himself, so there's no point in repeating that for a second or third time. You yourself, you're testifying now. Mr. Agnes has already testified. Why did you decide to use Mr. Agnes as an informer, and what information did you expect to get from him?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My decision to take him on as an informer was exclusively guided by his proposal and desire to get me in touch with the individuals whom I had ascertained he, in fact, could get me in touch with. For that, you don't need credibility of any kind. So my sources of information are also criminals or people who have been convicted of certain offences, and I expected that he could perhaps give me some information related to another contact that he could schedule for me, which he did not do. He did not put me in touch with anybody. This does not mean that I need not -- that I would not perhaps decide to call him as a witness one day in the proceedings here. So I think that that would be my answer to the question posed by Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So following up from that -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Following up from that, Mr. Avramovic, you are quite content to use an unreliable, as you put it, informer; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, an informer is somebody who can be very unreliable but who can give you a piece of information which you check out later on. It's a contact man, somebody who puts you in touch with somebody else, who informs you about something, and it is up to you to determine the truth of the information you've been given. So an informer is a well-known category in any proceedings and in preparing a defence case as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And I take it informers are usually rewarded for their efforts, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends what subject and before what organs and institutions. If you're thinking about informers officially working for certain services, then I can only assume that they are remunerated for their work, depending on the service which has engaged those individuals to provide them with information. But when we're talking about a defence case, this is done on a voluntary basis, absolutely, and something which is left to the personal discretion of the individual, whether he wishes to do so or not. So you must behave towards these individuals according to the book and according to the principle of voluntariness. And if they wish to do so, they do; and if they don't, they don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And Mr. Agnes was going to do this from the goodness of his heart for one of the people who was present when he was detained; is that it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot enter into his motives, nor can I explain his motives fully. I said a moment ago that his motives could be through the friendship that he had with Ms. Marosevic. Why shouldn't an individual, quite simply, be held in that status regardless of whether he was a detainee? That is my view, and that is what I decided to do in October 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'll move on. Sir, you've told us that you shared office space with Mr. Pantelic and Mr. Vukovic, is that correct, in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there's some other colleagues -- I apologise, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: There were some other colleagues. Okay. You would share office space, share expenses, share phone lines, share secretarial maybe?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could say that the majority of the things you enumerated, the sort of logistics of it, are shared.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But you have separate practices?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But in a collegial setting, would you help each other out? For example, if somebody was sick or on holidays or tied up in trial, would you assist each other with each other's cases?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In practice, we can always ask for a replacement of any lawyer who is not able to attend trials. In concrete terms, I always can and have the right to ask somebody -- some of my colleagues to replace me in a trial and that is something that we avail ourselves of, but we always take an expert, theoretically viewed, and hypothetically. I'm answering your question hypothetically. For example, if somebody who could replace me was in my own environment, then I would ask him to replace me at a trial or anything else, at some proceedings before a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, the questions I'm about to pose to you are not technical, they're not hypothetical, and I'm going to direct them specifically. Did you have the kind of working relationship with your colleagues, your -- I won't call them partners because that has another legal expression, but with your colleagues in practice, that you would assist each other?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it that way. I think that we all worked for ourselves as individual private practices.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: But you knew about each other's cases?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would socialise, of course, outside the office as well, and we would exchange information about our clients or potential cases which we decided to take on. We're friends, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And Milan Simic's case was one of those cases that you discussed?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you have in mind the defence of Milan Simic, then myself and Drago Vukovic were involved in that case from the very beginning, and when I was officially appointed his assistant, we did talk about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic knew what you were up to as well, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did, of course, know the case that I was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And would you discuss the names of potential witnesses with your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in exchanging information about our work and in exchanging the knowledge that we came by sometimes, it would be possible sometimes to impart information about potential witnesses as well or individuals which could give you information. I would tell that to my colleague Mr. Pisarevic were that relevant for his client.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sure. Now, I suggest to you, sir, that you had discussions with Mr. Agnes about a rehearsal programme that you wanted him to attend, didn't you? A rehearsal of evidence.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A rehearsal of testimony that I heard for the first time through his statements. That is when I first learned that type of terminology; that is to say, between myself and Mr. Agnes it was never a topic of discussion, nor was I able to understand what it meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, didn't you discuss with him that there would be a time when he would come for a week and someone would pretend to be a Prosecutor and someone would pretend to be a Defence counsel and his evidence would be rehearsed? Didn't that happen?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never discussed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, sir, Mr. Agnes is not a lawyer, is he? To your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: How would he know about such a programme of rehearsed evidence unless someone had talked to him about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think I am going to object to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, I think that's more in the form of a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, it's a comment that I would ask the witness to -- yes, you're right. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think it's a matter for us to make that assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You're right. Well, let me go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Now, at the time when all of this occurred in, say, April and May, there was a scheduled trial date for this case, was there not, the 22nd of June? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time in May, at a conference which was held, I think, on the 27th, 8th, or 9th of April, a trial date had been set for the 23rd, I think, of June. Yes. I remember that quite well. That was the first time I learnt that the trial would begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, I'd suggested to you that you had, in fact, discussed with Mr. Agnes, that there was such a programme of rehearsal and that your colleagues knew about it. I suggested that to you and you denied it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I absolutely deny something I never talked about nor discussed. And at the end, when I learnt about the trial, I didn't see that man again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Sir, did you listen to the tape of the telephone conversation of the 10th of May, 1999, where there is a discussion with your colleague Mr. Pantelic, followed by a discussion with you? Did you listen to that tape, all of it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We dealt with this, and that portion of the tape is not part of the evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: My response is: Not yet. It's now quite clearly an issue of credibility, and I'm about to launch my cross-examination of this witness on the basis of the foundation which I have just laid on the issue of credibility of an extremely significant issue, that there is reference in the portion of the tape referring to a programme. Mr. Pantelic, in that tape, actually talks about the timing of the programme being changed, and he calls him by the name "Daki."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Haynes, if my recollection is correct, you yourself, in your examination of this witness, you referred to this conversation, and it is normal, it is quite pertinent for the cross-examination to refer to it. I think that this kind of objection should not be repeated frequently. The cross-examination fits within the framework of the examination-in-chief, even if it has not been admitted into evidence. I think that you should not raise this kind of objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry if anything in my examination-in-chief was misleading or was not easy to follow, but I think Your Honour will find that the telephone conversation I referred to was the one between Mr. Agnes and Mr. Avramovic and only that conversation, and there can be no sensible suggestion that that is inadmissible, and I do not suggest it's inadmissible, and if he needs to be cross-examined about that, then he can be. But we're now moving into an area where the conversation referred to is between Mr. Agnes and a third party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the problem. You see, it was excluded before, or at least it was not admissible because it looked as if it was seeking to involve Mr. Pantelic in some form of contempt, and that had been a matter that had been dealt with at some earlier stage. Well, this evidence now goes in as a fact relevant to credit, not to show that Mr. Pantelic has been guilty of contempt but to show there was some discussion about a rehearsal. Why is it not admissible as hearsay evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I say it's not admissible because it's a conversation between Mr. Agnes and a third party, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So what?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it's not something upon which this witness can properly comment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No. No, no. He's not being asked to comment on the fact of the conversation but the truth of what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Then that would make it pure hearsay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If he says he knows nothing about it, that's the end of the cross-examination, but it would not make the rest of the tape inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, we have considered this matter. We think that there is a sufficient foundation for the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I think we better think about the practicality of this then, because at the moment, we, none of us, have heard it in evidence in this case, nor seen any transcript of it in any language. It's simply not part of the evidence. It hasn't been moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The tape is primed and ready to go. I have transcripts of it, and the original transcript, I believe, has already been filed and is in evidence before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I haven't seen the documents that came in with that tender. But it's certainly a document that I have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. And my friends have a copy of the tape -- my friends have a copy of the tape itself. They've heard the entire tape. They've had this for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I wasn't seeking to suggest that as a matter of fact this had not been disclosed, I was seeking to discover how this is going to affect the course of these proceedings, whether it is to be adduced as evidence now or as some form of rebuttal in due course, and of course it raises the very obvious possibility if not probability that the Defence will be calling a further witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Mr. Ryneveld, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: To repeat my question, sir, did you listen to the tape, all of it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Including the portion between "Daki" -- and just so we're clear, that's Mr. Agnes; correct -- and "Igor"?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But may I just make a brief comment? I heard the tape at Mr. Morrison's, who was my Defence counsel at the time, who took that document on a tape recorder he had in his apartment, and the truth of the matter is that I focused on the part of the conversation between me and Mr. Daki or, rather, Agnes. So I did hear it but I didn't really pay full attention to every detail of that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: No problem, sir. I think it's only about 30 seconds long.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I propose to have the first minute or so of the tape played for the portion. I have copies of the transcript for the assistance of the Chamber, and I believe my friend has copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I think we all have copies because notwithstanding the ruling that was made earlier on, the transcript of both of these telephone conversations went into the evidence anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: For ease of location --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you have those transcripts passed up?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voice-over] "Daki: Hello. Daki speaking. Hello. Hey, who's is on the phone? "Igor: It's Igor. Hello. Yes, yes. "Daki: Hey, where's Bani? "Igor: Hello. "Daki: Bani. Bani, where is Bani? "Igor: Call him on his mobile: 207. "Daki: 207 203. "Igor: That's right, call him. "Daki: And where is he? "Igor: He's in Belgrade. "Daki: Can I get him there? I've been calling him for an hour at that number, 207 203. Do you understand me? "Igor: What did you say? "Daki: I have been calling him at 207 203 for about an hour. I can't get through. Well, I can't get him. What? "Igor: Yes, yes. Well, call him later in the afternoon, or he will be in Samac on Tuesday. "Daki: In Samac on Tuesday? Hey, Igor, listen. When does that programme with Bani start? "Igor: That will be towards the end of the year. "Daki: Okay. I was in contact with him and he mentioned May, mid-May. "Igor: That doesn't matter. It's not urgent yet. "Daki: All right. I'll call Bani and arrange it with him. "Igor: Try to get hold of him in the afternoon. Okay. "Daki: Goodbye."

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Do you recall hearing that conversation, sir? Were you able to hear it -- no, Daki, quite clearly? That's Mr. Agnes; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: "Igor," that's your colleague Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: The phone number referred to, that's your phone number, 207-203?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: And you see that Mr. Agnes asks Mr. Pantelic, "When is that programme with Bani start?" And the answer was, "Towards the end of the year," or words to that effect, I'm paraphrasing. "Daki, I was at your place with him and now he's something about May, mid-May." What programme does that refer to, sir, if it isn't the rehearsal programme that Mr. Agnes talked about?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very difficult to answer that question with complete certainty on the basis of what I have just heard, and it is a good thing that you have reminded me of this because I said a moment ago that the last time I listened to this, I didn't pay any attention to this part. Mr. Agnes, it seems to me, uses the word "programme", and he says "in May." Mr. Pantelic, as far as I was able to understand, says it's not May but some other date. That is what I heard. What was implied, what is he asking him about which programme and what Mr. Pantelic understood him to mean, it is very difficult for me to give you a very unequivocal answer. From what I have heard, I am not convinced that this has anything to do with a programme of rehearsal. Even now that I've heard it -- maybe I should hear it once again to see whether any mention of a rehearsal is made -- only the word "programme" is used. And what Mr. Agnes means under that word addressing Mr. Pantelic, and what Mr. Pantelic meant when he gave him his answer, it is really difficult for me to give you a clearcut answer, under oath, to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm not asking you what Mr. Pantelic had in mind. I'm asking you, sir, what do you think that Daki, Mr. Agnes, was referring to when he said, "That programme with Bani that was first discovered about May, mid-May"? Do you know of any programme with Bani, you, with Daki in mid-May?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no programme agreed between him and me linked to any kind of trial or any methodology of work, if that is what you are asking me. That is something I never discussed with him, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a complete answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So you deny that there was a programme, despite what Mr. Agnes said on the phone to your partner, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Between me and Agnes, there was no programme planned in the sense that you are implying. Perhaps he is trying to provoke Mr. Pantelic. I really don't know. He uses slang a lot anyway, so I don't know. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's move on to something that you should know something about. That's the conversation that you had with Daki later on in the phone call. When he said, near the end of the phone call, and I'm sure you'll refresh your memory -- page 3 near the bottom, My Lords -- "All right, then. So there's no --" I'm sorry, back up a little bit. Daki: Hey, listen. I definitely need the money. Did you hear me? Bani: What? Daki: Do you understand me? You know the situation is I have nowhere to go, apartment, this or that. Bani: I shall send you -- And then there is an unintelligible portion. Daki: We'll sort it out. Bani: Unintelligible. Daki: Tomorrow afternoon? Bani: Unintelligible. Daki: Ah-hah. Bani: Unintelligible. Daki: All right. If it should be or you call you, that is, I shall call you, you know when to come. All right, get in touch with her. Our -- And then there is nothing further. Then the answer: Daki: All right. So there is no problem about the money? Bani: We'll be in touch through her. A couple of questions arising out of that. Who is "her"?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jasna Marosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: What was the money?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear for the first time in my life in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: You had never heard the reference to money in the conversation when you heard the tape played last time?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I told you that this was the first time in my life and in contact with him that I heard him mention money. No, I didn't say I hadn't heard it. Of course, I heard it and I read it, although there are certain corrections to be made in the transcript that I've drawn Mr. Haynes' attention to, and he tried to intervene and to correct the transcript, because that transcript has not been correctly translated. That is the problem. And this is a highly-relevant fact, and that relevant fact is linked to my answer to the question. What? Because it is the first time I hear him mention such a thing on the phone, and, anyway, I never heard it, and my answer is, "I'll call you," without wishing to chase him away and to hang up. In translation of that transcript, it says, "I'll send it," which is not what I said. "I'll call you." The meaning of the whole conversation is we'll see each other in Bosanski Samac, through her, so as to talk about what I assumed he wanted to discuss, and that is his existential problem, because that is what he had told me at the meeting in April. Therefore, neither did I promise him anything, nor did I in any way intimate a positive solution to his requests. That is the only fact that I can quite definitely state my opinion about. His comments are leading. That is, he is saying something that I have not said in my answers. What I keep saying is, "I'll call you when I get to Bosanski Samac." Furthermore, that transcript doesn't contain some other parts which I have managed, in cooperation with my Defence team, to reconstruct, and that is why Mr. Haynes has suggested that those texts be amended to be a correct translation of the conversation. That is the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have a copy of the translation that your counsel has provided me, and I can assure you I have no difficulty with that going to the Court. But in the translation that you have provided or in the translation that the Court now has, do you see anything in the conversation with Mr. Agnes and you whereby you say, "What the heck are you talking about, money?" Did you say anything like that to him? Did you ever say, "What do you mean, money?" Did you say that to him? Sorry, sir. "Yes" or "No" would really help. Did you say it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know you would like me to give you such an answer, but I would need to have a complete transcript, a translation of everything that the two of us said. And as important parts of sentences are missing in this translation, you're asking me to say "Yes" or "No", and I'm telling you that from our conversation, one could adduce that regarding the question he's asking me, my answer is, "We can talk about it when we see each other, because I don't know what you're talking about." He may have had a contact. Maybe he needs reimbursement of expenses he has had. Maybe he needs some other service from me that he would convey to me in person but not by telephone, and that is why I refused to discuss that subject. He is making leading questions. What the agreement was is for us to see each other in Bosanski Samac and to discuss the matter, because these are things I never discuss by telephone. That is the point, and that is why I am saying, once again, one has to bear in mind two things; the contents and the circumstances of the conversation. I tried to explain yesterday the circumstances, and today I am giving you the answers regarding the contents of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: So your response to the reference to money and an apartment is, "We will talk about it and we'll get in touch with Jasna, through Jasna"; is that it?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say that we will discuss at Jasna's what he mentions at the beginning without being specific. I cannot give him an answer to that question when I don't see any explanations. That may be a question of expenses. It may be a quite insignificant matter that we need to discuss. But as the transcript is obviously devoid of significant parts, I cannot give you an authoritative answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we should move on now, Mr. Ryneveld.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to move on to sitting down. Those are my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Those are your questions. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, since Mr. Ryneveld says he has no difficulty with the amended transcript that we've provided --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- I've only got two copies at the moment. I wonder if I could lead --

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I have one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: That's a clean copy that you provided me, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I think logically they should be Exhibit 1B, the Prosecution translation having been Exhibit 1A.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Perhaps my friend could clarify, but I believe just the changes are in bold print, as I understand it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, don't start --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Don't commence yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, we have seen the document that you have presented representing the translation of the conversation. What the Chamber will do is bring it to the attention of the official translators of the Tribunal and ask them to comment in particular on certain portions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm a little confused as to how I should proceed now, then. Would you prefer that the re-examination of Mr. Avramovic be deferred until tomorrow afternoon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I think you should proceed, I think you should proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are we going to be told how this particular translation was brought into being? I know that Mr. Avramovic has said that he made certain suggestions to you, but did you have somebody independent translate it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The history of the document is that the Prosecution translation was handed to us the morning, I think, that it was played.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you say "the Prosecution translation", it was, in fact, done by the official translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that's as it may be, but it was the first sight we had had of the translation, and it was just before the morning it was played. We had the tape listened to, and we made suggested amendments. I don't proffer any criticism, but, in fact, that document has been in the possession of the Prosecution for in excess of a month now, and we invited them to agree that there were supplements to the translation and corrections. Until now, we had received no answer. The answer, it appears, is they have no difficulty with that. I assume they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No difficulty with us saying it was the words. I don't know what that quite means, but it wasn't an acceptance of its accuracy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, that was why it was submitted to them several weeks ago, so that they might consider its accuracy. I'm afraid I took that as a concession that it was accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, what was it intended to be, Mr. Ryneveld?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Thank you. My friend gave it to me at the close of one of the days. I must take full responsibility. It was given to me. It was shuffled into my briefcase, along with a number of other papers, and frankly I did not have it translated. It was brought to our attention again, I believe, today, and I indicated that I had not had an opportunity to have it checked out. But we did look at the documents and thought that the changes did not -- were not of great significance to my cross-examination. So I had no objection to the Court seeing it or even considering it. But I cannot vouch for its accuracy, because apart from receiving it, yes, I admit well in advance I did not have it sent to the official translators for verification. But I didn't want to take paltry advantage of the fact that I hadn't had it checked to prevent my friend from at least introducing it. So in that respect, I take full responsibility that I am unable to do anything more than say to you I have no objection to it going in. I cannot, of course, vouch for its veracity or correctness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Mr. Haynes, you haven't really revealed the source of your translation. Was it an independent translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It was in house, in effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's hardly independent. The answer to it is it was not independent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. I mean the difficulty is, with this particular piece of evidence, that there are actually three sources to it. Mr. Agnes has given evidence about what he says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We're worried about the accuracy of this transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You haven't had it done independently, so that all we need to do, then, is to have it checked, for our translators to say, "Well, it could be that," or, "It is not that."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm happy that that is done. I don't know in what time scale that can be achieved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I believe that can be done very expeditiously. Proceed with your re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Mr. Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Dealing with the question of the blue bag briefly, when the blue bag was handed to you, that was, you say, in September?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the 17th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In vague terms, did you have any idea where Mr. Agnes was at that time?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of September, I assumed that he was probably in the Netherlands. I wasn't sure of that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did it appear to you at that stage he was likely to want to come back and reclaim his belongings that were in that bag?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The proceedings were ongoing, so I really couldn't assess what would happen. But I must believe that I didn't believe that he would come to pick up his things, as the proceedings were under way and I knew he was here, so I didn't expect him to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you actually take anything out of the bag on the day that it was handed to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't take anything. I put it away in the way I have told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, one other thing. Going back a year to September of 1998, if we may, there was a hearing in the trial on indictment between September the 2nd and September the 4th, I think, of 1998; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Prior to that date, what charge had Milan Simic faced?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Milan Simic was charged for events in the elementary school or, rather, for an event in which Milan Simic allegedly participated in beating up certain people. That would be the charge in brief, in summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: After the hearing in early September 1998, what charge did he then face?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the Status Conference or the hearing that was held at the beginning of September, the accused pleaded on the amended indictment in which the charges were expanded with respect to Milan Simic to include the charge of persecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How did that change in the charge that he faced, from an isolated incident to one of persecution, affect your decision to meet Mr. Agnes in late September of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I must rise. Didn't we cover this before in chief, and how does it arise out of cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Was there any cross-examination upon this, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I believe there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You believe. I don't. At least I don't remember it. But I'm happy to accept your assurance if you're right, but I certainly don't remember it. What was the nature of the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The nature of the cross-examination was that Drago Vukovic, having formed certain impressions of the witness that were unfavourable, there would thus be no point in Mr. Avramovic going to see him and see what he had to say. The point is that there had been a material change in the case between the time that Drago Vukovic had seen him and when Mr. Avramovic first saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: We heard that in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Nextly, Mr. Avramovic, dealing with the question that was put to you earlier on, you understand the meaning of the word "lure"?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that Mr. Agnes was to lure Mirsad Sahanic to come to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, between May -- between September of 1998 and May of 1999, did you have a lot of work to do in relation to the preparation of the trial and indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I think we heard that ad nauseam.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't think we did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Haynes. We must try to conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you do a lot of work in relation to the trial and the indictment between September of 1998 and May of 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me answer your question very briefly. In professional terms, that period in my life was, in the first place for my family, a very difficult one, because I had entirely forgotten my family and dedicated my entire time to the case. Because of the facts I had to prepare and to produce for this Trial Chamber, I worked literally daily from 7.00 until 10.00, 11.00 at night. I worked virtually all Saturdays and very many Sundays. I worked non-stop on travel and in the office. I spent on the case and the indictment at least 10 to 15 hours a day, and I devoted everything to that case. In fact, I lost my clients. I lost everything that I had been building up in my career because I wished to give my all to this case. And I sacrificed even my family. And now I understand Mr. Vukovic, when he realised at the beginning of September where further involvement in this case would take him. We in the Defence, Mr. Haynes, have very modest possibilities compared to the Prosecution. We have very limited staff to deal with such a complex charge as persecution. If the indictment had remained unchanged when the proceedings had started, it would have been an easier undertaking. But to delve into the issue of persecution, such a very broad charge is a very difficult one, so that my life was exclusively devoted to that task. That is, frankly, what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, again, just briefly if you can, how difficult is it to find people to tell you what happened in Bosanski Samac in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extremely difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You spoke to Mr. Agnes on the 28th of September, and you formed the view that he might be useful for information. What was the basis of that view that you took?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis for my view was the wish, through him, to reach potential new witnesses for certain events. And when I said a moment ago that it is difficult to find witnesses, what I meant was something that I need to explain. The environment in which the events allegedly occurred, according to the indictment, is a very small community. It is a community in which it is very difficult to do anything without these things being revealed, so that it is very difficult to work in such an environment. The charge is broad. There are many witnesses. The Defence had contact with many. The Defence can prepare in a qualitative manner for the case, but I'm saying that it is very hard to work because of the scope of the charges in the indictment. And also this is not in my own town, so that I have to travel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you were -- spoke to Mr. Agnes on the 28th of the September and he looked at lists and indicated that he knew some people, what expectation did you have that he would be able to get in touch with people?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time I didn't have any special expectations, because he himself showed reservations as to the success with these contacts. But, of course, I did hope that if he succeeded in doing so, it would be a good thing. It would be a good thing if we were able to reach more credible or completely credible witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In the scheme of things, after the 28th of September, how important was he to you in the conduct of this case?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you, quite frankly, that I have a lot of people like him on hold, so to speak, so that he is not a key source of information, so I didn't devote any particular attention to him. That is being very frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just lastly, because of something that appeared in the transcript earlier on, after you spoke to Jasna Marosevic, I think you said in about October of 1998, was there any possibility that he would be called as a witness in the defence of Milan Simic?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was my stand as Defence counsel for Milan Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Avramovic, the Chamber has a question for you. It relates to the report done by the senior legal officer of the billing records which were submitted to the Registry. A copy of the senior legal officer's report was submitted to you and to Mr. Haynes. I'm going to pass a copy to you and ask you to identify from the pseudonyms which one relates to Mr. Agnes. Pages 3, 4, and 5 contain the pseudonyms?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have looked through this document, and the pseudonyms are on the last page; that is to say, page 5. They are the dates the 22nd of September and the 28th of September. Those are the pseudonyms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That relate to Mr. Agnes?

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course, because there are no other witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: BRANISLAV AVRAMOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is no other witness from Mitrovica, so then that is sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before we adjourn, I think we have to make an assessment. Mr. Haynes, how long will your witness be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I see no reason to dissemble. My last witness is Mr. Simic. He will be short in chief, but I would have thought it unrealistic to suppose that in total he'll be much less than an hour, I suppose. The spectre has been raised today of a further witness being called, and thereafter some documents need to be introduced into evidence before I close my case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The further witness is to deal with the transcript of the telephone conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That would not be long, would it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And how long would your address be, your submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I wouldn't have thought they would be much less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Ryneveld, how long do you think your cross-examination will be, and what is the estimate of your time for your address?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: Since I have asked Ms. Paterson to deliver the closing address, I've just asked her, and she tells me less than an hour. I think we can assume up to an hour and that's safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So realistically, we should try to find some time beyond tomorrow afternoon's session, although we should try as hard as we can to see how far we can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I suppose the other possibility that's certainly been raised with me by the senior legal officer is that if we do need to look for another date, perhaps a substantial amount of closing statement could be put into written form. Again, I want to be completely up front. The submissions I make are going to be substantially evidentiary in their nature, but also they're going to touch upon the scope of Rule 77 itself, and I wonder whether that might be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we'll take the adjournment now, and tomorrow we'll make the assessment. In the meantime, the Chamber will make an effort to see whether there is any possibility for any session to be held on Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can I make a request that is utterly selfish and it really dictates whether I'm going to be burning the midnight oil tonight, and that is: Does the Chamber envisage hearing closing oral arguments tomorrow or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We would like to take it as far as possible, certainly. We would like to have this case concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Oh, I understand that, and so would I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And concluded this week, so that we would be making efforts to try to see whether it's possible to fit something in on Friday. It will be very difficult, but we'll try. But in the meantime, we have to try to finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Haynes, if I understood well, you have another witness who will not take very long for you. You said -- how much will your witness take, the examination-in-chief of Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A very short period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RYNEVELD
utterances.text: I'm sure that's going to depend on what he has to say, but I would imagine up to half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then perhaps we could try and finish tomorrow afternoon. I'm speaking in my own name, but I think we should make an effort to finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Judge Bennouna has spoken for the Chamber. We'll make every effort to conclude tomorrow afternoon. So we adjourn until 2.30 tomorrow. Mr. Avramovic, you are reminded that in the adjournment, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He's finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. You are released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
